[MATH: y = (x-7)(x+4)]
and we wish to translate this curve by [MATH: 2] units to the right.

Content:
Recall that to shift the curve [MATH: y = f(x)] by [MATH: 2] units to the right, we add [MATH: 2] to each [MATH: x]-coordinate to get the corresponding point on the new curve [MATH: y = g(x)]. So, the [MATH: x]-coordinates of the points on the new curve are given by

[MATH: x = x_{\textrm{new}} - 2.]

To get the equation of the new curve, we substitute this into the equation of the first curve. Doing this, we get

[MATH: y|= (x − 7)(x + 4); y|= ((x_{new} − 2) − 7)((x_{new} − 2) + 4).]

[MATH: y = ((x - 2) - 7)((x - 2) + 4).]

Finally, simplifying the expression, we have
[MATH: y|= ((x − 2) − 7)((x − 2) + 4); y|= (x − 2 − 7)(x − 2 + 4); y|= (x − 9)(x + 2).]

Therefore, we conclude that
[MATH: g(x) = (x-9)(x+2).]

[MATH: x = x_{\textrm{new}} + 2.]

Content:
In this lesson, we will learn how to transform polynomial functions by shifting their graphs and determining how these shifts affect their properties.

Content:
Suppose a curve is defined by [MATH: y = f(x),] where
[MATH: f(x) = (x-7)(x+4).]
If [MATH: y = g(x)] is a horizontal translation of [MATH: y = f(x)] by [MATH: 2] units right, how can we find [MATH: g(x)?]

Content:
We're given the curve
[MATH: y = (x-7)(x+4)]
and we wish to translate this curve by [MATH: 2] units to the right.

Content:
Recall that to shift the curve [MATH: y = f(x)] by [MATH: 2] units to the right, we add [MATH: 2] to each [MATH: x]-coordinate to get the corresponding point on the new curve [MATH: y = g(x)]. So, the [MATH: x]-coordinates of the points on the new curve are given by

Content:
[MATH: x_{\textrm{new}} = x + 2.]

Content:
This equation is equivalent to

Content:
[MATH: x = x_{\textrm{new}} - 2.]

Content:
To get the equation of the new curve, we substitute this into the equation of the first curve. Doing this, we get

Content:
[MATH: y|= (x − 7)(x + 4); y|= ((x_{new} − 2) − 7)((x_{new} − 2) + 4).]

Content:
Dropping the [MATH: \textrm{new}] suffix, we get
[MATH: y = ((x - 2) - 7)((x - 2) + 4).]

Content:
Finally, simplifying the expression, we have
[MATH: y|= ((x − 2) − 7)((x − 2) + 4); y|= (x − 2 − 7)(x − 2 + 4); y|= (x − 9)(x + 2).]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that
[MATH: g(x) = (x-9)(x+2).]

Content:
We can check that this answer makes sense by examining the roots of both functions:

Content:
- From the equation
[MATH: f(x) = (x-7)(x+4)]
we can see that the roots are [MATH: x=7] and [MATH: x=-4.]
- From the equation
[MATH: g(x) = (x-9)(x+2)]
we can see that the roots are [MATH: x=9] and [MATH: x=-2.]
- Thus, we can see that the roots have shifted two units right under the transformation.
